correctness.rationale: For H an arbitrary spanning disjoint union of simple cycles of length at least 9, G=H complement has degree N−3, so fewer than N−3 initially blue vertices permit no first force. For three white vertices, a first force exists precisely when two white vertices are the H-neighbors of a blue midpoint v; after the first force, distinct neighborhoods on long cycles ensure the remaining two white vertices can be forced sequentially. Thus minimum zero forcing sets correspond bijectively to allowed white triples containing a distance-two pair of H with midpoint excluded. The distance-two graph D is 2-regular and triangle-free. Inclusion–exclusion yields N(N−4) allowed triples. Pair multiplicity g(a,b) for distances 1,2,3,4,other is 2,N−3,4,3,4; summing C(g,2) over pair classes yields edge count N(C(N,2)−11). Degree sums of pair multiplicities split into classes N,N+1,N+2,2N−6, with multiplicities 2N+10c10, 2N−20c10, N(N−9)+10c10, N; ten-cycles uniquely merge the ±5 antipodal choices. Core-exchange paths give diameter ≤3, disjoint allowed triples yield ≥3. Independently simulated actual graph zero forcing and all minimum triple exchanges, graph degree spectra, pair counts and diameter for cycle lists [9],[10],[11],[12],[9,9],[9,10],[10,10]; agreed exactly with formulas. The all-size theorem is based on the structural counting and exchange paths, not finite enumeration.

value.rationale: The complete exchange degree spectrum of minimum zero forcing sets is a natural refinement of the zero-forcing number and scalar minimum-set count. Its exceptional dependence on ten-cycle components provides a genuine recoverable structural invariant invisible to exchange graph order, size, and diameter. A complete classification for every disjoint union of long cycles is a motivated theorem about forcing-set reconfiguration.
